title: The Voyage Continued
imageAlt: Selected sequence: Mactan in 1521, surviving expedition members continued, and Victoria returned to Spain under Elcano in 1522. Magellan did not complete the return.
content:
Mactan was not the end of every expedition member's journey. Surviving members continued sailing after Magellan's death. Your first task is to distinguish the death of a leader from the end of a voyage.

In 1522, the ship Victoria returned to Spain under Juan Sebastian Elcano. This completed the expedition's first circumnavigation: a journey around the world. Magellan had led the earlier part of the expedition, but he did not live to complete the return. Many people contributed to the voyage; it was not one person's journey alone.

Watch how to correct a report. Keep the event at Mactan in 1521, the continuation by survivors, and the return in 1522 in separate boxes. Connect them in order. Do not write that Magellan personally returned after his death, or that all the original participants returned together.

The diagram shows selected events, not a complete route or list of crew members. Use its sequence to explain continuity and change: the voyage continued, while its leadership and surviving crew changed.
clues: A leader and a voyage
Magellan died at Mactan in 1521. That does not mean every expedition member died there.
A later return
Victoria returned to Spain under Elcano in 1522, completing the circumnavigation.
Collective effort
Distinguish earlier leadership from the returning crew's achievement. Do not claim every original participant returned.
task: Which report correctly explains the continuation after Mactan?
Survivors continued, and Victoria returned under Elcano in 1522
Magellan returned to Spain after dying in 1521
Every original participant returned on the same day
All later voyages ended at Mactan
reason: The expedition continued after Magellan's death. Victoria's return under Elcano in 1522 completed the circumnavigation.
definition: A journey all the way around the world.

title: Put the Later Expeditions in Order
imageAlt: Selected expedition departure years: Loaisa 1525, Saavedra 1527, Villalobos 1542. Dates identify departures, not identical arrival dates or one continuous voyage.
content:
Several later expeditions followed the Magellan-Elcano voyage. They were separate journeys, not three names for the same fleet. This mission follows a selected timeline, not every voyage in the Pacific.

Loaisa's expedition departed in 1525. Saavedra's departed in 1527. Villalobos's departed from Mexico in 1542 and reached the Philippine region the following year. A departure date tells when a journey began; it is not automatically the date of arrival.

Try this worked example. To put the cards in order, compare the years: 1525 comes before 1527, and both come before 1542. Next, read what each date labels. Keep a departure in one year separate from an arrival in another.

The purpose is to understand repeated attempts over time, not memorize every ship name. Your report should name the selected order and state a limit: a timeline does not show that each expedition followed an identical route, achieved its aims or gained control of the communities it encountered.
clues: Separate voyages
Loaisa, Saavedra and Villalobos identify distinct expeditions, not one crew changing its name.
Departure order
Read the selected departure years as Loaisa 1525, Saavedra 1527, then Villalobos 1542.
Read the date label
Villalobos departed in 1542 and reached the Philippine region in 1543. Departure and arrival are different events.
task: Which ordering correctly uses the selected departure dates?
Loaisa, then Saavedra, then Villalobos
Villalobos, then Loaisa, then Saavedra
Saavedra and Villalobos were one expedition in 1525
All three departure dates are dates of arrival at the same island
reason: The selected departures were Loaisa in 1525, Saavedra in 1527 and Villalobos in 1542. Read departure and arrival dates separately.
definition: The order in which events happened.

title: Why Keep Sending Voyages?
imageAlt: A planning guide separates a voyage aim, practical challenges such as supplies and a return route, and evidence of its outcome. An aim is not guaranteed success.
content:
Why send another expedition after a difficult voyage? Spanish sponsors remained interested in trade, routes and influence in Asia. An earlier journey could reveal possibilities without solving every practical problem.

Crossing an ocean in one direction did not automatically supply a reliable route back across the Pacific. Voyages also needed food, water and working ships. Communities already living in the places visited could cooperate, negotiate or resist. European claims and rivalry did not remove those communities' own interests.

Use a fictional planning table. Put an aim in one column: reaching trade connections. Put requirements in another: supplies and a workable return. Put evidence of the actual result in a third. A sponsor's wish belongs under aims; it is not evidence that the wish was achieved.

Compare the columns before judging a voyage. Repeated attempts show continuing interest, but the number of departures alone does not prove lasting control. Nor does difficulty make all participants' actions harmless. Ask what happened to the people and places involved as well as the ships.
clues: An aim
Sponsors continued to seek trade access, routes and influence. These are aims, not proof of achievement.
A practical challenge
An outward crossing did not automatically solve the return journey. Supplies and ship condition also mattered.
An outcome to check
Use evidence of what happened. Repeated voyages do not by themselves establish local consent or lasting colonial control.
task: Which comparison helps explain repeated voyages responsibly?
Separate trade and route aims from practical challenges and actual outcomes
Treat every sponsor's wish as an accomplished result
Count departures as proof that every community agreed
Assume crossing once solved every return journey
reason: Continuing trade and route interests encouraged attempts, but supplies, return routes and local responses affected what happened.
definition: Something a person or group wants to achieve.

title: Villalobos and a Name on the Record
imageAlt: The name Filipinas is linked to Villalobos's expedition in 1543 and Prince Felipe. A separate limit states that a name does not create a community or establish consent to rule.
content:
Villalobos's expedition left Mexico in 1542 and reached the Philippine region in 1543. The name Filipinas became associated with this expedition, honoring Prince Felipe, later Philip II of Spain. It was initially applied to part of the islands and later used more widely. Do not imagine a single ceremony where every community suddenly chose one national name.

A naming record tells us about the people who used the name and the connection they wanted to make. It does not mean that they created the islands or the communities living there. Local people already had histories, languages and names for places.

Try a fictional museum-label task. A label says that using a royal name made all residents accept foreign rule. Separate the supported naming connection from that extra claim. A name in an expedition account does not establish everyone's agreement.

Your explanation can link Villalobos, the 1540s and Prince Felipe while keeping the limit clear: naming is different from settling, governing or receiving consent from the people of every island.
clues: A naming connection
Filipinas is associated with the Villalobos expedition and Prince Felipe, later Philip II.
Changing scope
The name was used for part of the islands before its use spread more widely. It was not an instant decision by all communities.
An important limit
An outsider's name does not create a place's history or establish residents' consent to foreign rule.
task: Which exhibit label uses the naming evidence carefully?
Filipinas is linked to Villalobos's expedition and Prince Felipe; the name does not prove universal consent
Villalobos created the islands by naming them
All communities adopted one name at a single national ceremony
A royal name proves immediate control of every island
reason: The naming connection honors Prince Felipe. Its use does not mean local history began then or that every community accepted foreign rule.
definition: Evidence showing how a person or group used a name for a place.

title: Arrival Is Not the Same as Colonial Rule
imageAlt: Evidence questions distinguish arrival, a recorded name and continuing colonial institutions. None alone proves that all communities were under effective control.
content:
An expedition is an organized journey with a purpose. Colonial rule involves an outside power establishing and maintaining authority over a place and its people. These are connected topics, but the words do not mean the same thing.

A ship's arrival is evidence of a visit. A name in an account is evidence of naming. To explain continuing colonial rule, investigate settlements, governing institutions, resources, force, agreements and local responses over time. A visit or claim alone cannot answer all those questions.

Legazpi's expedition reached Cebu in 1565 and established a Spanish settlement there. This is a later development, not something accomplished by Magellan in 1521 or Villalobos in 1543. The next chapter examines how colonial rule developed and how people responded. One settlement still did not mean instant control of every island.

For this fictional report check, classify the evidence before drawing a conclusion. Ask whether it shows arrival, naming or continued authority. Keeping these separate helps you explain change without erasing local choices or resistance.
clues: A journey
An expedition can reach a place without establishing continuing colonial institutions there.
A later development
Legazpi's arrival and settlement in Cebu in 1565 belong to a later stage, studied in the next chapter.
Control has limits
Even a settlement does not establish immediate, effective control of every community. Check places and responses over time.
task: Which evidence would help investigate continuing colonial rule beyond a visit?
Evidence about settlements, institutions and local responses over time
Only a ship's arrival on one day
Only an outsider's name for a place
Only the order of expedition departure years
reason: Arrival and naming are different from continuing colonial rule. Examine settlements, institutions and local responses over time.
definition: Authority established and maintained over a place and its people by an outside power.

title: Complete Your Expedition Comparison
imageAlt: A selected comparison timeline labels expedition departures separately from later arrivals. It does not declare a chapter badge earned or all communities colonized.
content:
Build a comparison rather than a list of names. First, connect the survivors' continued voyage with Victoria's return under Elcano in 1522. Next, order the selected later departures: Loaisa, Saavedra and Villalobos. Explain why an aim, a difficult return route and an outcome belong in different columns.

Use the naming clue carefully. The connection between Filipinas and Prince Felipe does not erase older local histories or prove consent. Then separate arrival from the later establishment of continuing colonial institutions.

Try this report frame in your own words: After Mactan, [supported continuation]. Later expeditions [selected sequence]. Their aims did not guarantee [outcome]. Naming evidence supports [specific connection], but not [unsupported claim]. This is a teaching frame, not an original historical quotation.

Use the mission quiz to check what you learned. If a topic is difficult, revisit its lesson and try targeted practice before another quiz attempt. Passing earns the mission reward once. Complete all missions, then pass the chapter challenge to earn the chapter badge.
clues: Connect the sequence
Distinguish the continued Magellan-Elcano voyage from separate later expeditions.
Compare aims and results
A trade aim, a recorded name and an arrival need different evidence from a claim about continuing rule.
Keep the next step honest
The remaining chapter challenge and later chapters must be prepared before their completion can be claimed.
task: Which report best connects the mission ideas?
Voyages continued, aims faced constraints, and naming or arrival did not establish universal colonial rule
Every later leader commanded the same fleet in the same year
A recorded name proves that all communities agreed to be ruled
Magellan personally returned in 1522 and began a modern republic
reason: Compare chronology, aims and outcomes. Keep the meaning of a name or arrival separate from evidence of continuing colonial rule.
definition: Examining similarities and differences between things using clear points of evidence.
